voice_event.text:
To us Jesus is what the whole church says he is - fully God, fully man, crucified under Pontius Pilate, raised on the third day. That was never our own quarrel, not with Rome and not between our own two cities. What is distinctly ours is what we were taught his death secures. God's own free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved - not anything foreseen or earned. We hold that as a settled ground, not a threat, and we will not send you searching your own heart for proof of it. Our own confession says it plainly:

"We reject those who seek, apart from Christ, whether they are chosen... Let... Christ be the mirror in which we behold [our] predestination".

What we actually have of Christ is not a living chain. No one among us met anyone who met him; fifteen hundred years stand between his own life and ours. What we have is the text, and we hold that it is enough on its own terms.

voice_event.text:
He died once, for all, and that sacrifice is never repeated. Our own founder said it plainly: Christ sacrificed himself once. That sacrifice is, to eternity, of endless value and redeems forever all the sins of all believers. What Rome called the mass, we refused to call a sacrifice at all - the altar became a table, because what happens there is not a death repeated but a death remembered and its benefit truly given.

He also secured, by that one death, everyone God chose before the world began. Not by their own choice made first, and not by anything foreseen in them - by his own free will alone. That is what his death accomplished, and it is why we point away from the self toward him when someone asks whether they are among the chosen.

voice_event.speaker: rzg
voice_event.text:
Scripture alone, not church tradition or a pope's decree, is the final authority for our doctrine and our civic order. Zurich enacted this through public debate; Geneva enacted it through sustained teaching. Both cities hold the same conviction.

Our own founder said so of himself, and we hold it as our own rule still: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better - but only from the Scriptures themselves, not from a chain of memory we do not possess and do not need.

The words themselves - sola scriptura - are Latin, meaning 'by Scripture alone.' The conviction came first; the phrase itself followed as a way to name what we had already begun testing. At Zurich, that conviction was argued aloud, before the whole city, until the council itself said what the text had yielded. At Geneva, it was built up article by article, taught to everyone, and tested against how a believer actually lives.

Our own founder stated it directly in his first public defense:

The articles and opinions below, I, Ulrich Zwingli, confess... If I have not now understood [Scripture] rightly... I will allow myself to be taught better, but [only] from the aforesaid Scriptures.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: rzg
voice_event.text:
We believed Scripture alone is sufficient because we believed God himself had spoken plainly enough in it that no pope's decree, no council's vote, and no custom handed down unexamined could stand against what the text itself yields. The reason was theological before it was institutional: if God spoke, and spoke clearly enough to be heard, then adding a second authority alongside it - tradition, or a living voice claiming to interpret it - would be to say God had not spoken clearly enough after all.

Both our cities tested this the same way, though they enacted it differently. Zurich argued it aloud, before the whole assembled city, until the council itself judged what the text had yielded. Geneva built it up article by article, taught it to everyone, and tested it against how a believer actually lives. The conviction was the same; the method was not borrowed.

One real challenge tested whether the method itself was enough. The Anabaptists, who had once stood with Zwingli, pressed the same scriptural method further and read it to mean a church gathered only by a believer's own profession, apart from the whole city. We did not deny they read Scripture. We denied they read it whole.

voice_event.speaker: rzg
voice_event.text:
Heinrich Bullinger lived it out across four decades at Zurich, from the day Zwingli died at Kappel until 1575. He held the office of Antistes - Zurich's own senior pastor, answerable to the city council. He did not invent the conviction; he carried it forward after the man who had. What Scripture alone warranted, he taught. What it did not, he refused. That steadiness across forty years, through war's aftermath and the work of holding two cities together in one doctrine, is the closest thing we have to someone who simply lived the rule rather than arguing for it first.

He also wrote the clearest single line we have on where to look when the doctrine of election presses too hard:

"We reject those who seek, apart from Christ, whether they are chosen... Let... Christ be the mirror in which we behold [our] predestination".

That is Bullinger's own voice, not our founder's, and it shows what living the conviction looked like in pastoral practice - not searching the self for proof, but pointing away from it toward the promise given.

voice_event.text:
That two cities can hold one conviction without holding one arrangement, and we never tried to flatten that into agreement where it was not. Scripture alone warrants what we teach and how we order our churches - both Zurich and Geneva held that from the beginning. But who finally holds authority over church discipline, we never settled between ourselves. Zurich's council governed church and city together from our first days. Geneva's own Consistory only won its independence from that kind of claim by 1555. Neither side conceded the question to the other. We hold that unresolved, because it is also true.

The same honesty runs through what we teach about the Supper. In 1549, worried whether Geneva's and Zurich's own teaching actually agreed, Calvin travelled to Zurich himself rather than trust a letter, and what he and Farel worked out there became the Consensus Tigurinus. Both cities signed it. Whether that agreement deepens our founder's earlier word or only restates it more carefully, we do not claim to know. We hold both statements as our own, without resolving which is the last word.
